vignette:
# Khalid

Khalid has been working for the regional transit authority for six years, and for most of that time, he genuinely loved his job. There was something satisfying about the rhythm of it—the precision required to manage schedules, the responsibility of keeping hundreds of passengers safe, the camaraderie with his crew. He'd worked his way up from assistant conductor to lead conductor on the evening commuter line, a position that carried real authority and respect.

The evening of March 14th started like any other. Khalid was conducting the 6:47 p.m. run, checking tickets, moving through the cars with practiced efficiency. The train was moderately full—office workers heading home, students with backpacks, an elderly woman with shopping bags. At the third stop, a man in his fifties boarded, agitated and muttering. Khalid noticed but thought nothing of it; he'd encountered plenty of difficult passengers over the years.

Three stops later, as the train accelerated out of the station, the man suddenly stood and began shouting at another passenger—a young woman in her twenties who had, apparently, accidentally bumped into him. What started as verbal escalated with shocking speed. The man grabbed her arm, and when she tried to pull away, he shoved her hard against the window. Khalid moved toward them immediately, his voice steady as he told the man to release her. But in the moment Khalid reached them, the man's fist connected with the woman's face. She screamed. Blood streamed from her nose.

Khalid managed to physically separate them, and the woman stumbled backward into a seat, trembling and crying. He radioed for police while keeping himself between the aggressor and the victim, his heart pounding so hard he could barely focus on the radio. The man lunged at him, and Khalid had to physically restrain him until the train pulled into the next station and officers boarded.

The woman was taken to the hospital. Khalid gave his statement. Everyone told him he'd done the right thing, that he'd handled it professionally. He believed that, intellectually. But something inside him had fractured.

Now, four months later, Khalid finds himself hypervigilant in a way that exhausts him. Every passenger boarding his train feels like a potential threat. He scans faces obsessively, looking for signs of aggression—clenched jaws, sudden movements, raised voices. His body stays tense throughout his shifts. When passengers argue about seating or fares, his chest tightens and his breathing becomes shallow. Twice he's had to step into the crew cabin to calm himself down.

Sleep has become difficult. He lies awake replaying the moment the man's fist connected with the woman's face, wondering if he could have prevented it, whether he should have noticed the danger sooner. When he does sleep, he dreams of the screaming, of blood, of his own helplessness. He wakes with his sheets soaked through.

Outside of work, Khalid has withdrawn significantly. His friends have noticed he's distant, that he cancels plans. Loud noises—car horns, doors slamming, even raised voices at the grocery store—make him flinch violently. He's started taking longer routes to avoid the transit station, which feels ironic and frustrating given that he works there. He loves his job, or he did, but now the thought of boarding that train fills him with dread.

He hasn't told his family much about what happened. His mother would worry, and he doesn't want to burden her. Instead, he carries this alone, wondering if he's overreacting, if he should simply be able to move past it by now.
